title: Trump: Rep. Sessions, son of Mogilevich attorney, stalls Russian sanctions bill
description_short: Trump: Rep. Sessions, son of Mogilevich attorney, stalls Russian sanctions bill
description_medium: Representative Pete Sessions sought to delay a Russia-sanctions bill in the House in June 2017 after it had passed the Senate with overwhelming support. Sessions said he objected to provisions that could disadvantage American energy companies. The legislation also required congressional review before the president could loosen specified sanctions.
description_long: On June 29, 2017, Representative Pete Sessions sought to slow a Russia-sanctions bill that had passed the Senate with broad support. The legislation would require congressional approval before the president could remove or alter specified sanctions. Sessions objected to provisions he said could disadvantage American energy companies. The Trump administration also pressed lawmakers to change the measure, which constrained presidential discretion over sanctions. Pete Sessions's father, William Sessions, worked as an attorney and lobbyist for Russian businessman Semion Mogilevich. The family relationship formed part of the public context around the congressman's position, but does not by itself show that Mogilevich influenced it. Congress ultimately passed a revised bill, which Trump signed in August 2017. The episode was an effort to delay or alter the bill, not to prevent its enactment. The immediate legislative dispute centered on the balance between executive authority, congressional oversight and the effect of sanctions on U.S. businesses.

title: Trump: Barr names Durham ‘special counsel' to investigate the Russia probe
description_short: Trump: Barr names Durham ‘special counsel' to investigate the Russia probe
description_medium: Attorney General William Barr appointed John Durham as special counsel on October 19, 2020 to continue investigating the origins and conduct of the Russia inquiry. Durham had already been examining related matters since 2019. The appointment gave the investigation a regulatory status intended to protect it from termination without specified grounds during a change of administration.
description_long:
Attorney General William Barr appointed John Durham as special counsel on October 19, 2020 to continue investigating the origins and conduct of the Russia inquiry. Durham had already been examining related matters since 2019. The appointment gave the investigation a regulatory status intended to protect it from termination without specified grounds during a change of administration.

Durham could examine whether officials or others violated laws through intelligence, counterintelligence or law-enforcement activities directed at the 2016 campaigns and related people. Under Justice Department regulations, the attorney general could remove a special counsel for misconduct, dereliction of duty or conflict of interest, with a written explanation.

The appointment itself did not prove that the earlier FBI investigation was fabricated or that its participants committed crimes. It authorized examination of those questions. Barr’s appointment established a mandate, appointed a prosecutor and provided conditions governing removal; it did not determine whether the earlier FBI investigation was fabricated or whether its participants committed crimes.

title: Trump: ‘Money grab': Trump and Musk's DOGE steal $80M from NYC
description_short: Trump: ‘Money grab': Trump and Musk's DOGE steal $80M from NYC
description_medium: In February 2025, federal authorities reversed more than $80 million in FEMA payments to New York City. The money had been approved to reimburse migrant shelter and care costs. City comptroller Brad Lander said his staff discovered the withdrawal without prior warning and challenged its legality.
description_long:
In February 2025, federal authorities reversed more than $80 million in FEMA payments to New York City. The money had been approved to reimburse migrant shelter and care costs. City comptroller Brad Lander said his staff discovered the withdrawal without prior warning and challenged its legality.

The reversal followed Elon Musk’s criticism of payments he characterized as funding luxury hotels for migrants. New York later sued to recover the money, arguing that the government opposed the purposes for which funds had been appropriated and awarded. City officials described both a financial loss and concern about further unilateral withdrawals.

New York’s lawsuit and the administration’s reversal left the legality of the action contested; the episode was not a final judicial finding of theft. The claim about luxury hotels was disputed, and the litigation’s outcome remained unresolved.

title: Trump “couldn’t care less” if foreign automakers raise prices due to tariffs
description_short: Trump “couldn’t care less” if foreign automakers raise prices due to tariffs
description_medium: In a March 2025 NBC interview, Donald Trump dismissed concerns that foreign automakers would raise prices following his announcement of 25 percent tariffs on imported vehicles. He argued that higher prices would encourage buyers to choose American-made cars and manufacturers to move production to the United States. The statement presented price increases as an acceptable part of his trade strategy.
description_long:
In a March 2025 NBC interview, Donald Trump dismissed concerns that foreign automakers would raise prices following his announcement of 25 percent tariffs on imported vehicles. He argued that higher prices would encourage buyers to choose American-made cars and manufacturers to move production to the United States. The statement presented price increases as an acceptable part of his trade strategy.

Trump said the tariffs were intended to remain in place and denied having instructed automobile executives to avoid raising prices. His explanation emphasized where cars were manufactured: producing them in the United States, he argued, would avoid the vehicle tariff. Tariffs on imported parts could also raise costs for cars assembled domestically, complicating the distinction between imported and American-made vehicles. The episode captures the administration's stated economic rationale and its response to prospective consumer costs. It does not establish that every manufacturer raised prices, quantify the final cost to individual buyers, or show that production relocation actually followed. At the time of the interview, the final consumer-price and production effects remained uncertain.

title: Trump: Banks give Donald Trump a $450k monthly allowance to pretend to be rich
description_short: Trump: Banks give Donald Trump a $450k monthly allowance to pretend to be rich
description_medium: In June 1990, banks negotiating a rescue of Donald Trump's finances agreed to a $65 million loan and limits on his personal spending. The arrangement included a $450,000 monthly ceiling for household and personal expenses that year. The agreement illustrates the severity of Trump's liquidity problems and the lenders' effort to keep his businesses operating under financial restrictions.
description_long:
In June 1990, banks negotiating a rescue of Donald Trump's finances agreed to a $65 million loan and limits on his personal spending. The arrangement included a $450,000 monthly ceiling for household and personal expenses that year. The agreement illustrates the severity of Trump's liquidity problems and the lenders' effort to keep his businesses operating under financial restrictions.

About seventy banks participated in the syndicate, and the arrangement deferred payments on $850 million of debt. Income from the relevant properties would go to lenders while those obligations remained subject to the arrangement. Personal spending limits were scheduled to decline to $375,000 a month in 1991 and $300,000 in 1992. The apparently lavish allowance was thus part of a negotiated restriction rather than evidence that Trump had unrestricted cash. The banks had an interest in preventing a disorderly collapse that could reduce recovery on their loans. The agreement concerned private financing: continued loans and spending controls were negotiated to avoid a disorderly collapse and protect lenders’ recovery.

The outbreak, centered in Gaines County, West Texas, killed two unvaccinated children in Lubbock with no underlying health conditions, and one adult in New Mexico — the first U.S. measles deaths in over a decade. Overall hospitalization rates reached 11–13%, with children under 5 hospitalized at a 23% rate. Experts cited declining vaccination rates (92.7% kindergarten MMR coverage, below the 95% herd immunity threshold) and RFK Jr.'s anti-vaccine messaging as contributing factors; by August 2026, cases had risen to 2,465 across 47 states.
context.recovered_rationale: This matters because the documented measles resurgence produced deaths, substantial hospitalization, and spread across much of the country, while vaccination coverage fell below the stated herd-immunity threshold. The record indicates a public-health protection gap affecting children especially severely and identifies anti-vaccine messaging as a contributing concern, making prevention capacity and official health communication central accountability issues.

title: Trump promises to defund social security, give himself a tax cut if he's re-elected
description_short: Trump promises to defund social security, give himself a tax cut if he's re-elected
description_medium: Donald Trump announced pandemic-related executive measures in August 2020 that included a temporary payroll-tax deferral and additional unemployment assistance. He also said he would seek to make the tax relief permanent if reelected. Critics warned about the implications for programs financed through payroll taxes, while questions remained about repayment and the authority for lasting changes.
description_long:
Donald Trump announced pandemic-related executive measures in August 2020 that included a temporary payroll-tax deferral and additional unemployment assistance. He also said he would seek to make the tax relief permanent if reelected. Critics warned about the implications for programs financed through payroll taxes, while questions remained about repayment and the authority for lasting changes.

The tax measure concerned withholding during the remainder of the year, rather than a completed permanent repeal of the tax. Deferral can produce temporarily larger paychecks while leaving obligations to be addressed later, making it different from an unconditional tax cut. The measures included FEMA funding for supplemental unemployment benefits and prompted debate about Congress’s spending authority. Opponents argued that the proposal threatened Social Security funding, but the executive action did not abolish the program. Claims that Trump’s businesses could benefit did not quantify a personal gain. The announcement established a temporary deferral and a campaign promise to pursue permanent relief, not a completed permanent tax change.

Its findings concerned political statements made through her official position. The Hatch Act restricts certain partisan activity by federal employees, making the official context of Conway's statements central to the case. The findings concerned Conway’s criticism of Democratic candidates and conduct that continued after earlier warnings. Conway publicly dismissed the report, while Trump's response shielded her from the recommended personnel action. The OSC finding described repeated violations; the count depends on how individual statements and acts are tallied. The dispute centered on the president’s refusal to act on a recommendation involving his own adviser, not on enforcement of the Act in every case. The episode brought into focus the gap between a formal ethics finding and the president’s response to the recommended consequence.

title: Donald Trump letter accuses street vendor veterans of destroying the city
description_short: Donald Trump letter accuses street vendor veterans of destroying the city
description_medium: In June 2004, Donald Trump wrote to New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg about street vendors working near Trump Tower. Trump described Fifth Avenue as “deplorable,” said the vendors were “rapidly destroying” the street, and questioned whether some were veterans. He asked the mayor to address vendors near his property. The letter’s claims about military service were accusations by Trump, not findings by city officials.
description_long: On or shortly before June 17, 2004, Donald Trump sent New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg a letter about street vendors near Trump Tower. Trump called conditions on Fifth Avenue “deplorable” and said the vendors were “rapidly destroying” the street. He also questioned whether some vendors who identified themselves as veterans had served in the military. The letter asked the mayor to address the vendors, placing a complaint about the area around Trump’s property before city government. Trump’s letter brought a property owner’s complaint about nearby street activity directly to the mayor. His statements about the vendors’ military service were allegations, not findings by city officials.
